title: Prevention for children, older adults & special groups
blurb: Tailoring prevention to babies and children, pregnant women, older adults, people with disabilities, orthodontic patients and the medically compromised.
question: In one morning you see a 7-year-old who 'brushes on his own', a pregnant woman with morning sickness and bleeding gums, and an 80-year-old with arthritic hands, a partial denture and decay on exposed roots. How would your preventive advice differ for each?

teach.body: Fluoride, sugar control and plaque removal protect everyone, but how you deliver them depends on the patient's age, health, abilities and circumstances. DBOH sets out advice by age and adds extra measures for patients giving concern, including people with disabilities, medical conditions, frailty or dry mouth. Differences in culture, language, diet and access to care also affect how disease shows up and how well advice works, so you adapt to the person in front of you.

teach.h: Children: prevention through the early years

items.label: Parent brushes twice daily: smear, 1,000+ ppm
Introduce a free-flow cup; no sugar added to foods
Pea-sized amount; varnish twice a year
First molars erupt: seal if giving concern; 1,350–1,500 ppm from 7

teach.caption: Bottles should hold only breast milk, formula or cooled boiled water. Take children to the dentist when the first teeth appear.

teach.body: Parents or carers should brush young children's teeth, and help and supervise as they get older, especially at night. Most children can't brush well alone until around 7, and many need help for longer. Advise minimising sugary foods and drinks, avoiding sugar at bedtime and using sugar-free medicines. DBOH supports breastfeeding, exclusively for around the first 6 months. For children giving concern, the dentist may advise 1,350–1,500 ppm toothpaste, more frequent varnish, fissure sealants and a shorter recall.

Hormonal changes exaggerate the gums' reaction to plaque, so pregnancy gingivitis (red, bleeding gums) is common, and occasionally a pregnancy epulis develops. Good plaque control is the answer. Morning sickness bathes teeth in acid: advise rinsing with water or a fluoride mouthwash afterwards and not brushing straight away, as the enamel is softened. Cravings can mean more sugary snacks. In England, NHS dental care is free during pregnancy and for 12 months after the birth, so encourage attendance.

More people now keep their natural teeth into old age. Gum recession exposes root surfaces, which decay more easily than enamel (root caries). Many medicines cause dry mouth, reducing saliva's protection. Arthritis, stroke or dementia can make brushing hard, and frail or care-home residents often rely on carers. For active root or coronal caries the dentist may prescribe 2,800 or 5,000 ppm toothpaste. Dentures should be cleaned daily, left out overnight and marked with the person's name in care settings.

teach.h: Matching the aid to the need
head: Need
Helpful aid or advice
rows: Powered brush with small head; wide or foam handle
Careful brushing at brackets, interdental and single-tufted brushes
Carer brushes, standing behind, with a set routine
Sip water, sugar-free gum, high-fluoride paste if prescribed

teach.body: People with physical or learning disabilities, and medically compromised patients, are patients giving concern in DBOH. Support brushing with carer help, specialised brushes or non-foaming toothpaste, ask the GP for sugar-free versions of long-term medicines, apply varnish regularly and shorten recalls. Diabetes raises periodontitis risk, especially if poorly controlled. Head and neck radiotherapy and some cancer treatments cause severe dry mouth and high caries risk. Some patients need referral to special care dental services.

teach.h: Quick reference: key risk and focus
head: Group
Main risk
Prevention focus

teach.text: A 7-year-old who 'brushes on his own' still usually needs help. Parents should supervise and assist, especially at night, until the child can brush effectively; leaving young children to it unsupervised is a common cause of missed brushing.

items: Children: parent brushes then supervises (especially at night) until around 7+; smear under 3, pea-sized from 3.
Pregnancy: gingivitis is common; after vomiting rinse, don't brush straight away; NHS care free in England.
Older adults: root caries and dry mouth; high-fluoride paste on prescription; clean dentures daily.
Reduced dexterity: powered brush with a small head or adapted handles.
Braces: careful brushing round brackets plus interdental aids.

summary: You can now tailor preventive advice for babies and children, pregnant women, older adults, people with disabilities, orthodontic patients and medically compromised patients, choose suitable aids for different needs, and explain how culture, health and circumstances change the advice you give.

A.q: A parent says their 7-year-old brushes alone and often misses the evening brush. What is the best advice?
options: Let the child brush longer alone
Brush in the morning only for now
A.why: Children usually need a parent to supervise and help with brushing, especially at night, until they can brush effectively.

whyNot.0: Longer unsupervised brushing doesn't solve missed or poor brushing.
whyNot.1: Night-time brushing is the most important session.
whyNot.3: Mouthwash doesn't remove plaque and isn't a substitute for brushing.

A.q: A patient with reduced manual dexterity struggles to brush. What is the best recommendation?
options: A powered brush with a small head
Brush less often to save their effort
A.why: A powered brush with a small head does much of the work and is easier to manage with limited dexterity.

whyNot.0: A hard brush risks abrasion, and a large head is harder to control.
whyNot.2: Brushing less often increases plaque and disease risk.
whyNot.3: Flossing doesn't replace brushing or fluoride delivery.

A.q: A pregnant patient has morning sickness. What advice should you give about brushing?
options: Stop brushing until the sickness ends
Use a harder brush for a while
Rinse with water, then brush later
A.why: Acid from vomiting softens enamel, so rinsing first and not brushing immediately helps avoid wear.

whyNot.0: Brushing softened enamel straight away can wear it.
whyNot.1: Brushing should continue twice daily; just not immediately after vomiting.
whyNot.2: A harder brush would increase wear on softened enamel.

B.q: A patient with fixed orthodontic braces has bleeding gums around the brackets. What advice is best?
options: Brush at brackets, use interdental aids
Brush once a day to reduce the irritation
Wait until the braces are removed
B.why: Plaque gathers around brackets, so careful brushing there plus interdental aids removes it and lets the gums heal.

whyNot.1: Brushing less often lets more plaque build up.
whyNot.2: Mouthwash doesn't remove plaque from around brackets.
whyNot.3: Waiting allows gingivitis and decay to develop under the appliance.

B.q: Why are older adults with gum recession at higher risk of decay?
B.why: Recession exposes root surfaces covered by cementum and dentine, which decay more easily than enamel.

whyNot.0: Enamel doesn't thicken with age; it can wear.
whyNot.2: Saliva often decreases, especially with medicines.
whyNot.3: Fluoride protects teeth at every age.

B.q: In England, how long is NHS dental care free for a woman after she gives birth?
B.why: NHS dental care in England is free during pregnancy and for 12 months after the baby is born.

whyNot.0: 6 weeks is far shorter than the actual entitlement.
whyNot.1: The entitlement lasts longer than 6 months.
whyNot.2: It doesn't extend to two years.

C.q: What should a baby's bottle contain, according to DBOH?
options: Breast milk, formula or cooled boiled water
Any drink at all, as long as the bottle stops at 3
C.why: DBOH advises that bottles should contain only breast milk, infant formula or cooled boiled water.

whyNot.0: Fruit juice contains free sugars and acid.
whyNot.2: Squash can still contain sugars and acids.
whyNot.3: Bottle feeding should be discouraged from 1 year, and drinks should be limited to milk or water.

C.q: A care home resident wears a partial denture. What denture advice is correct?
options: Clean it once a week in very hot water
Clean daily and leave out overnight
Soak it in bleach every night
C.why: Dentures should be cleaned every day and left out overnight to rest the tissues and reduce infection.

whyNot.0: Weekly cleaning is not enough, and hot water can distort acrylic.
whyNot.1: Wearing dentures overnight increases the risk of denture stomatitis.
whyNot.3: Bleach can damage dentures, especially metal parts.

C.q: Which group does DBOH list among patients giving concern?
options: Adults with no history of decay at all
C.why: Children and adults with physical and learning disabilities are listed among patients giving concern.

whyNot.1: No decay history suggests lower risk.
whyNot.3: Not smoking is protective, not a risk factor.

reteach.title: Same toolkit, different hands
reteach.question: Imagine the same three tools, fluoride, less sugar and plaque removal, being handed to a toddler, a pregnant woman and an 80-year-old. What has to change for each?

blocks.body: For a toddler, the parent holds the brush and controls the toothpaste. For a pregnant woman, the tools are the same but her gums react more and sickness brings acid, so timing matters. For an 80-year-old with arthritis, the tools may need adapting, a powered brush or a wider handle, and their roots need extra fluoride. The message stays the same; who does it and how changes.

blocks.text: Don't assume an older adult has dentures or a child can brush alone. Ask and look, then tailor.

explain.body: Parents brush, then help and supervise, especially at night, until about 7 or older. Smear under 3, pea-sized from 3. Minimise sugar, no sugar at bedtime, sugar-free medicines, bottle only for milk or water.

test.q: From what age should babies be introduced to drinking from a free-flow cup?
test.why: DBOH advises introducing a free-flow cup from 6 months and discouraging bottle feeding from 1 year.

whyNot.0: 3 months is too early; solids and cups start around 6 months.
whyNot.3: 3 years is much later than advised.

explain.body: Hormones exaggerate the gum response to plaque, causing pregnancy gingivitis. After sickness, rinse with water or fluoride mouthwash rather than brushing straight away. NHS dental care is free in England during pregnancy and for 12 months after.

explain.caption: Pregnancy gingivitis: red, swollen gums that bleed easily. Plaque control is still the answer.

test.q: Why is gingivitis more common during pregnancy?
options: Fluoride works less well during pregnancy
Teeth lose calcium to the baby
test.why: Pregnancy hormones increase the gums' inflammatory response to plaque.

whyNot.2: Fluoride works the same in pregnancy.
whyNot.3: The baby doesn't take calcium from the mother's teeth; this is a myth.

explain.body: Recession exposes roots that decay easily; medicines cause dry mouth; dexterity and memory may decline. High-fluoride toothpaste may be prescribed. Clean dentures daily and leave them out overnight.

explain.caption: Gum recession exposes the root surface, which is softer than enamel and prone to root caries.

test.q: An older patient has active root caries. What might the dentist prescribe?
test.why: DBOH says 2,800 or 5,000 ppm toothpaste can be prescribed for adults with active coronal or root caries.

whyNot.0: A children's paste is lower strength than adults need.
whyNot.1: Removing fluoride would increase caries risk.
whyNot.2: Whitening paste offers no extra caries protection.

explain.body: Use adapted or powered brushes, non-foaming toothpaste where swallowing is difficult, carer-assisted brushing, sugar-free medicines, regular varnish and shorter recalls. Refer to special care dental services if needed.

head: Need
Aid
rows: Wide or foam handle, powered brush

test.q: A carer says the person they support gags on toothpaste foam. Which product could help?
test.why: DBOH suggests non-foaming toothpaste to support brushing for people who need help, such as those with swallowing difficulties.

whyNot.0: Whitening paste still foams and adds no benefit.
whyNot.3: Brushing without toothpaste loses the fluoride benefit.
